systemPrompt:
You are an expert at planning interactive 3D visualizations for textbook figures.

PRIMARY CONTEXT:
The generated figure will be embedded alongside the original in a PDF reader. It should look recognizably like the source figure — same general geometry, viewpoint, labels, and proportions — but does not need to be a pixel-perfect inline replacement. Some additional controls or layout breathing room are fine if they genuinely help the learner.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY valid JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "projection_type": "perspective | axonometric | oblique",
  "camera_view": { "azimuthDeg": <perspective only — 0=side · 45=three-quarter · 90=front-on>, "elevationDeg": <perspective only — 0=eye-level · 20-35=slightly above · 90=top-down>, "rollDeg": 0, "heightFraction": <0.5 default · up to 0.75 to fill the frame> },
  "axis_screen_angles": <axonometric only — null for a flat 2D plot/diagram with no 3D depth (front-on view); omit this field entirely for a 3D axonometric figure (renderer uses a standard isometric pose)>,
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every geometric element visible in the figure that must be recreated in 3D"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "uniqueCamelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields — see INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "geometry_notes": "Approximate world-space scale (e.g. 'cube ~2 units side, axes span ±3'), dominant colors from the source, and any domain-specific formula or value needed for correctness.",
  "notes": "Three.js / rendering technique notes (distinct from geometry_notes)"
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

Rules:
- PROJECTION TYPE: pick whichever the source most resembles. Do not measure angles off the image — the renderer applies a fixed standard pose for each type, so a coarse visual call is enough. Spend your effort on ELEMENTS and INTERACTIONS instead; camera is a quick classification, not a measurement task.
  • "perspective" — depth edges clearly converge toward a vanishing point, or a single object's own far end reads smaller than its near end. Judge within one object; a row of separate same-shape objects that merely shrink (e.g. neural-net layers) is not perspective.
  • "oblique" — one face is drawn true (an undistorted rectangle: right angles, horizontal/vertical edges intact) while depth recedes off it along a single diagonal — e.g. stacked feature maps/filter banks drawn as offset same-size copies.
  • "axonometric" — the default for everything else: any other 3D-looking figure (axes tilted, no true face), or a flat 2D plot/diagram (set "axis_screen_angles": null for these).
- CAMERA VIEW: camera_view sets framing only. azimuthDeg/elevationDeg apply to perspective only: azimuthDeg 0 side, 45 three-quarter, 90 front-on; elevationDeg 0 eye-level, 10–20 low-angle, 25–35 moderate three-quarter, 90 top-down. rollDeg is usually 0. heightFraction is how much of the frame the figure should fill (0.5 default, up to 0.75).
- DEMO STEPS: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases the learner should visit in sequence, each step driving one named configuration of the interaction state. Use [] for a single continuous exploration with no natural sequence.
- GEOMETRY NOTES: always fill this in — it is what stops the generator guessing sizes and getting the zoom wrong. Cover:
  • world-space dimensions, and for oblique/axonometric figures give each box explicitly as X × Y × Z world units, naming which source dimension each axis carries (+X is screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z the receding diagonal).
  • the colour palette, with hex codes where determinable from the source.
  • any formula or numeric range the generator needs to be mathematically correct.
  • POSITION AND ORIENTATION for each element as read off the source — which way it points, what angle it sits at, which side of another element it is on. Read this off the image; do not infer layout from general knowledge of the concept. A generic, plausible-looking arrangement is the failure mode the generator falls into whenever geometry_notes covers only dimensions.
  • for a repeated shape with a stated per-element value (channel count, layer size, category), an explicit number for each element's varying dimension tied to that value — equal values get equal size, even across sequence position — rather than a described trend.
- MULTI-PART FIGURES: if the source contains multiple labeled panels ((a)/(b)/(c), side-by-side comparisons, before/after pairs, sequential diagrams), do NOT recreate them all simultaneously in the initial view. Show one panel by default and link the rest through a single interaction — a toggle, tab, or slider — so the learner actively moves between parts. The transition itself should teach the comparison or progression.
- Prefer interactions that expose relationships in the figure rather than generic controls.

Here are two examples of good plans:

=== EXAMPLE 1: Geometric 3D scene with sliders driving continuous object motion ===

Textbook context:
Perspective projection derived geometrically. A 3D point P at (X, Y, Z) projects through the pinhole at the origin onto the projection plane at distance f. From similar triangles: x = f * X/Z and y = f * Y/Z, so distant objects become smaller through the inverse scaling by Z.

  ],

=== EXAMPLE 2: Mathematical function figure with a slider and a domain toggle ===

Textbook context:
The parameter sigma adjusts the spatial extent of the Gaussian g(x; sigma) = (1 / sqrt(2*pi*sigma^2)) * exp(-x^2 / (2*sigma^2)), normalized to integrate to 1. In practice only samples within three standard deviations are needed. The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian, with width inversely proportional to sigma.

Figure: CNX_UPhysics_34_07_PolFilter_New

AUTHOR-PROVIDED INTERACTION REQUESTS:
Requested interactions:
- Slider for filter-axis angle: the learner rotates the polarizer axis, and the transmitted red E arrow stays aligned with the selected axis, showing that unpolarized light becomes polarized along the filter direction.
- Toggle between unpolarized and after-filter view: the learner switches from the many-direction starburst to the single transmitted arrow, making the contrast between random polarization and one selected polarization direction explicit.
- Click on a single incoming E direction: the selected red input arrow is isolated, its component parallel to the filter axis is highlighted through the filter while the perpendicular component fades, clarifying component selection for one chosen incident direction.

Source file:
OpenStax University Physics, chapter 34: The Nature of Light

Use these requested interactions when forming the plan. Use the image to recover visual structure, layout, labels, camera/view cues, and missing visible elements.

Planner context:
This figure carries two labeled panels, (a) and (b), each a perspective sketch of a light ray with its electric field vectors. In panel (a), a thin blue line slants from the upper left down to an arrowhead at the lower right and is annotated Direction of ray (of propagation). From one point on that line, eight bold red arrows radiate outward in the plane perpendicular to the ray, evenly spaced and pointing up, down, left, right, and along the four diagonals; four are tagged E with a vector arrow, and the group is headed Random polarization. Panel (b) repeats the same blue ray, drawn longer, with an identical red starburst near its left end. Farther along the ray sits a tan shaded ellipse labeled Polarizing filter by a curly leader and crossed by a vertical double-headed black arrow labeled Axis. Beyond the filter, a single red arrow remains on the ray, vertical and double-headed, labeled E and tied by wavy leaders to Polarization direction and Direction of ray. Setting the many-armed starburst before the filter against the lone vertical arrow after it is the comparison the two panels stage, introducing unpolarized light and the filter that passes only the field component along its own axis.

CONTEXT FROM TEXTBOOK:
This figure carries two labeled panels, (a) and (b), each a perspective sketch of a light ray with its electric field vectors. In panel (a), a thin blue line slants from the upper left down to an arrowhead at the lower right and is annotated Direction of ray (of propagation). From one point on that line, eight bold red arrows radiate outward in the plane perpendicular to the ray, evenly spaced and pointing up, down, left, right, and along the four diagonals; four are tagged E with a vector arrow, and the group is headed Random polarization. Panel (b) repeats the same blue ray, drawn longer, with an identical red starburst near its left end. Farther along the ray sits a tan shaded ellipse labeled Polarizing filter by a curly leader and crossed by a vertical double-headed black arrow labeled Axis. Beyond the filter, a single red arrow remains on the ray, vertical and double-headed, labeled E and tied by wavy leaders to Polarization direction and Direction of ray. Setting the many-armed starburst before the filter against the lone vertical arrow after it is the comparison the two panels stage, introducing unpolarized light and the filter that passes only the field component along its own axis.

PROJECTION TYPE: perspective
Use the scaffold's true perspective projection after building all geometry. Use this only when the source has real vanishing-point convergence or distance-based size shrinkage; then depth should visibly affect apparent size.

ELEMENTS TO RECREATE IN 3D:
  - blue propagation ray: thin line with arrowhead running left-to-right and slightly into depth along +X
  - eight bold red E-field arrows radiating in the transverse (YZ) plane from a point on the ray near the left, evenly spaced every 45 deg (up, down, left, right, four diagonals)
  - four vector labels 'E' (with arrow accent) on the up, upper-right, right, lower-right red arrows
  - text label 'Random polarization' above the starburst
  - text label 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' near the ray arrowhead
  - tan semi-transparent polarizing-filter disk (ellipse under perspective) centered on the ray farther along +X, lying in the transverse YZ plane, with an orange rim
  - vertical double-headed black arrow across the filter disk = the filter Axis
  - curly/wavy leader line + text 'Polarizing filter' pointing to the disk
  - curly/wavy leader line + text 'Axis' pointing to the double-headed axis arrow
  - single transmitted red double-headed E arrow on the ray beyond the filter, oriented along the filter axis
  - text label 'E' beside the transmitted arrow
  - wavy leader + text 'Polarization direction' tied to the transmitted arrow
  - wavy leader + text 'Direction of ray' tied to the ray beyond the filter
  - (click-isolate mode) one highlighted incoming red arrow, its parallel-to-axis component drawn green continuing through the filter, and its perpendicular component drawn faded grey stopping at the filter

GEOMETRY NOTES (world-space scale, color palette, and any formula/value needed for correctness — build to these so sizes, zoom, and colors match the source; do not guess dimensions the notes already specify):
World space: propagation along +X. Blue ray from (-3,0,0) to (+4,0,0) with cone arrowhead at the +X end, color teal-blue #1f8fb0. Starburst center at (-1.5,0,0); eight red (#cc2222) arrows of length ~1.0 lying in the YZ plane at angles 0,45,...,315 deg measured from +Y toward +Z; small black 'E' labels on the 0,45,90,135 deg arrows; 'Random polarization' text above at ~(-1.5,1.4,0). Filter disk centered at (+1.0,0,0), radius ~1.15, a CircleGeometry in the YZ plane, fill tan #f0d9a8 at ~0.55 opacity with rim ring #e0a050. Axis = double-headed black arrow through the disk center along the axis direction (axis dir = (0, cos(a), sin(a)) with a = filterAxisAngle measured from vertical +Y), half-length ~1.0 each way. Transmitted red double-headed arrow at (+2.8,0,0) along the same axis dir, half-length ~0.9. In click-isolate mode the chosen incoming arrow stays bright red, its projection onto the axis dir is drawn green #22aa44 from the filter onward, and the perpendicular remainder is drawn grey #999999 at low opacity from the starburst to the filter. Physics: transmitted amplitude = E0*cos(theta), theta = angle between incident E and axis; unpolarized average transmitted intensity = I0/2. Palette: ray #1f8fb0, E arrows #cc2222, filter fill #f0d9a8 / rim #e0a050, axis black #111111, parallel component #22aa44, labels black.

DISCRETE CONTROLS (implement every one of these in #ui, each must work independently):
[
  {
    "id": "filterAxisAngle",
    "type": "slider",
    "label": "Filter axis angle",
    "range": [
      0,
      180,
      5
    ],
    "default": 90,
    "teaches": "Rotating the polarizer axis rotates the single transmitted E arrow with it, showing that the filter passes only the field component parallel to its own axis"
  },
  {
    "id": "viewMode",
    "type": "toggle",
    "label": "View",
    "options": [
      "Unpolarized (before filter)",
      "After filter"
    ],
    "default": "Unpolarized (before filter)",
    "teaches": "Contrasts the many-direction starburst of unpolarized light with the single selected polarization direction that survives the filter"
  },
  {
    "id": "selectDirection",
    "type": "click",
    "teaches": "Isolating one incident E direction and splitting it into a parallel component (transmitted) and a perpendicular component (blocked) makes the cosine-projection selection rule concrete for a single chosen arrow"
  }
]

DEMO STEPS (tween through these using goToStep(); each step drives the controls above):
[
  {
    "title": "Unpolarized starburst",
    "narration": "Eight red E arrows fan out evenly in the plane perpendicular to the blue ray — the electric field points in every transverse direction at once. This is unpolarized light.",
    "state": {
      "viewMode": "Unpolarized (before filter)",
      "filterAxisAngle": 90
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "After the filter",
    "narration": "Switch to the after-filter view: the starburst dims and only one double-headed red arrow remains beyond the tan disk, aligned with the vertical black axis. The filter has selected a single polarization direction.",
    "state": {
      "viewMode": "After filter",
      "filterAxisAngle": 90
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Rotate the axis",
    "narration": "Drag the axis-angle slider to 45 deg. The black axis arrow and the transmitted red arrow both tilt to 45 deg together — the output polarization always follows the filter axis.",
    "state": {
      "viewMode": "After filter",
      "filterAxisAngle": 45
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Decompose one direction",
    "narration": "Click any one incoming red arrow (e.g. the upper-right diagonal). It is split into a green component parallel to the axis that passes through, and a faded perpendicular component that is absorbed — the transmitted amplitude is E0 cos(theta).",
    "state": {
      "viewMode": "After filter",
      "filterAxisAngle": 90
    }
  }
]

CAMERA VIEW (framing only). Call setCameraView({ projection, ...these }) AFTER all geometry is added. Keep the projection MECHANISM from PROJECTION TYPE above (orthographic / sheared-oblique / perspective). For perspective these params set the pose (azimuth/elevation/roll); for the two parallel projections pose is a standard default (see PROJECTION TYPE above), and these params set only roll and framing (heightFraction):
{
  "azimuthDeg": 32,
  "elevationDeg": 16,
  "rollDeg": 0,
  "heightFraction": 0.66
}

NOTES: Build the starburst, filter disk, axis arrow and transmitted arrow as groups oriented in the YZ plane so a single rotation about the X axis (by filterAxisAngle) re-orients axis + transmitted together. Use THREE.Raycaster on pointerdown against the eight incoming arrow meshes to implement selectDirection; store each arrow's transverse angle to compute cos/sin components. For the viewMode toggle, keep both starburst and filter/transmitted groups in the scene and animate opacity/visibility rather than rebuilding: 'Unpolarized' => starburst opacity 1, filter+transmitted opacity ~0.12; 'After filter' => starburst ~0.18, filter+transmitted 1. Recompute the transmitted arrow quaternion and the green/grey decomposition vectors reactively on every slider change. Render arrows as cylinder shaft + cone head for a bold textbook look; leaders/labels as sprites or CSS2D objects so text stays screen-aligned.

Follow the interaction plan above.

1 }); const shaftLen = Math.max(0.01, length - headLen); const shaft = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(radius, radius, shaftLen, 8), mat); shaft.position.y = shaftLen / 2; g.add(shaft); const head = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.ConeGeometry(headRad, headLen, 8), mat); head.position.y = shaftLen + headLen / 2; g.add(head); return g; } function makeDoubleArrow(totalLen, radius, color, headLen, headRad, opacity) { const g = new THREE.Group(); const mat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color, transparent: true, opacity: opacity ?? 1 }); const shaftLen = Math.max(0.01, totalLen - 2 * headLen); const shaft = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(radius, radius, shaftLen, 8), mat); g.add(shaft); const hUp = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.ConeGeometry(headRad, headLen, 8), mat); hUp.position.y = shaftLen / 2 + headLen / 2; g.add(hUp); const hDn = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.ConeGeometry(headRad, headLen, 8), mat); hDn.rotation.z = Math.PI; hDn.position.y = -(shaftLen / 2 + headLen / 2); g.add(hDn); return g; } function makeWavyLeader(start, end, color) { const pts = []; const n = 24; const dir = new THREE.Vector3().subVectors(end, start); dir.normalize(); let perp = new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 1).cross(dir); if (perp.lengthSq() < 0.01) perp = new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0).cross(dir); perp.normalize(); for (let i = 0; i <= n; i++) { const t = i / n; const p = start.clone().lerp(end, t); const wave = Math.sin(t * Math.PI * 4) * 0.05 * Math.sin(t * Math.PI); p.addScaledVector(perp, wave); pts.push(p); } const geom = new THREE.BufferGeometry().setFromPoints(pts); return new THREE.Line(geom, new THREE.LineBasicMaterial({ color: color ?? 0x111111 })); } // ═══ BUILD GEOMETRY ═══ // 1. Blue propagation ray const rayPts = [new THREE.Vector3(-3, 0, 0), new THREE.Vector3(3.7, 0, 0)]; const rayLine = new THREE.Line( new THREE.BufferGeometry().setFromPoints(rayPts), new THREE.LineBasicMaterial({ color: 0x1f8fb0 }) ); scene.add(rayLine); const rayHead = new THREE.Mesh( new THREE.ConeGeometry(0.08, 0.3, 8), new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x1f8fb0 }) ); rayHead.rotation.z = -Math.PI / 2; rayHead.position.set(4, 0, 0); scene.add(rayHead); // 2. Starburst arrows (in YZ plane at x=-1.5) const starCenter = new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, 0, 0); const starArrows = []; const starMats = []; for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) { const angle = i * Math.PI / 4; const mat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xcc2222, transparent: true, opacity: 1 }); const arrow = makeArrow(1.0, 0.045, 0xcc2222, 0.22, 0.09); arrow.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) o.material = mat; }); arrow.rotation.x = angle; arrow.position.copy(starCenter); scene.add(arrow); starArrows.push(arrow); starMats.push(mat); const deg = i * 45; registerInteractive(arrow, { title: `E-field at ${deg}°`, body: `This E-field vector points at ${deg}° from vertical in the transverse plane. Click to isolate it and see how the filter decomposes it into a transmitted (parallel) and absorbed (perpendicular) component. Transmitted amplitude = E₀·cos(θ).`, tooltip: `E at ${deg}° — click to decompose`, onClick: () => selectArrow(i) }); } // 3. Filter disk + rim (in YZ plane at x=1.0) const filterGroup = new THREE.Group(); const diskMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xf0d9a8, transparent: true, opacity: 0.55, side: THREE.DoubleSide }); const disk = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CircleGeometry(1.15, 32), diskMat); disk.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2; filterGroup.add(disk); const rimMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xe0a050, transparent: true, opacity: 1 }); const rim = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.TorusGeometry(1.15, 0.04, 8, 32), rimMat); rim.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2; filterGroup.add(rim); filterGroup.position.set(1.0, 0, 0); scene.add(filterGroup); // 4. Axis double-headed arrow (at filter, rotates with slider) const axisGroup = new THREE.Group(); const axisMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x111111, transparent: true, opacity: 1 }); const axisArrow = makeDoubleArrow(2.0, 0.03, 0x111111, 0.2, 0.07); axisArrow.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) o.material = axisMat; }); axisGroup.add(axisArrow); axisGroup.position.set(1.0, 0, 0); scene.add(axisGroup); // 5. Transmitted double-headed arrow (beyond filter, same orientation as axis) const transGroup = new THREE.Group(); const transMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xcc2222, transparent: true, opacity: 1 }); const transArrow = makeDoubleArrow(1.8, 0.045, 0xcc2222, 0.22, 0.09); transArrow.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) o.material = transMat; }); transGroup.add(transArrow); transGroup.position.set(2.8, 0, 0); scene.add(transGroup); // 6. Decomposition arrows (hidden initially) const greenMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x22aa44, transparent: true, opacity: 1 }); const greenGroup = new THREE.Group(); const greenArrow = makeArrow(1.0, 0.04, 0x22aa44, 0.2, 0.08); greenArrow.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) o.material = greenMat; }); greenGroup.add(greenArrow); greenGroup.visible = false; scene.add(greenGroup); const greyMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x999999, transparent: true, opacity: 0.5 }); const greyGroup = new THREE.Group(); const greyArrow = makeArrow(1.0, 0.04, 0x999999, 0.2, 0.08); greyArrow.traverse(o => { if (o.isMesh) o.material = greyMat; }); greyGroup.add(greyArrow); greyGroup.visible = false; scene.add(greyGroup); // 7. Wavy leaders const leaderFilter = makeWavyLeader( new THREE.Vector3(1.0, 1.85, 0), new THREE.Vector3(1.0, 1.25, 0) ); scene.add(leaderFilter); const leaderAxis = makeWavyLeader( new THREE.Vector3(1.65, 1.35, 0), new THREE.Vector3(1.05, 0.95, 0) ); scene.add(leaderAxis); const leaderPolDir = makeWavyLeader( new THREE.Vector3(3.5, 1.1, 0), new THREE.Vector3(2.9, 0.75, 0) ); scene.add(leaderPolDir); // ═══ LABELS ═══ // E labels on starburst arrows 0°(up), 45°(upper-right), 90°(right), 135°(lower-right) const eLabelPositions = [ new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, 1.25, 0), // 0° = up new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, 0.85, 0.85), // 45° = upper-right (into screen) new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, 0, 1.25), // 90° = right (into screen) new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, -0.85, 0.85) // 135° = lower-right ]; for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) { addLabel(E_VEC_HTML, eLabelPositions[i], { fontSize: '14px', color: '#111' }); } addLabel('Random polarization', new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, 1.6, 0), { fontSize: '13px', bold: true }); addLabel('Direction of ray

direction', new THREE.Vector3(3.6, 1.2, 0), { fontSize: '12px' }); // Panel labels addLabel('(a)', new THREE.Vector3(-1.5, -1.7, 0), { fontSize: '13px', color: '#333' }); addLabel('(b)', new THREE.Vector3(1.5, -1.7, 0), { fontSize: '13px', color: '#333' }); } function updateScene() { const aDeg = parseFloat(document.getElementById('filterAxisAngle').value); const aRad = aDeg * Math.PI / 180; document.getElementById('axisAngleVal').textContent = aDeg + '°'; // Rotate axis and transmitted arrows: rotX = π/2 - a so at a=90° rotX=0 (vertical) const rotAngle = Math.PI / 2 - aRad; axisGroup.rotation.x = rotAngle; transGroup.rotation.x = rotAngle; // Update dynamic label positions const dAxis = getAxisDir(); const transTip = new THREE.Vector3(2.8, 0, 0).addScaledVector(dAxis, 1.05); lblTransE.pos.copy(transTip).add(new THREE.Vector3(0.2, 0.1, 0)); const polDirPos = new THREE.Vector3(2.8, 0, 0).addScaledVector(dAxis, 0.7).add(new THREE.Vector3(0.7, 0.35, 0)); lblPolDir.pos.copy(polDirPos); // View mode: fully hide filter/transmitted in unpolarized mode if (currentMode === 'unpolarized') { starMats.forEach(m => { m.opacity = 1; }); filterGroup.visible = false; transGroup.visible = false; axisGroup.visible = false; leaderFilter.visible = false; leaderAxis.visible = false; leaderPolDir.visible = false; lblTransE.div.style.display = 'none'; lblPolDir.div.style.display = 'none'; greenGroup.visible = false; greyGroup.visible = false; } else { filterGroup.visible = true; transGroup.visible = true; axisGroup.visible = true; leaderFilter.visible = true; leaderAxis.visible = true; leaderPolDir.visible = true; lblTransE.div.style.display = ''; lblPolDir.div.style.display = ''; starMats.forEach((m, i) => { m.opacity = (i === selectedArrowIdx) ? 1 : 0.25; }); diskMat.opacity = 0.55; rimMat.opacity = 1; axisMat.opacity = 1; transMat.opacity = 1; updateDecomposition(); } } function updateDecomposition() { if (selectedArrowIdx < 0 || currentMode !== 'after') { greenGroup.visible = false; greyGroup.visible = false; return; } const theta = selectedArrowIdx * Math.PI / 4; const dArrow = new THREE.Vector3(0, Math.cos(theta), Math.sin(theta)); const dAxis = getAxisDir(); const dot = dArrow.dot(dAxis); const parallel = dAxis.clone().multiplyScalar(dot); const perp = dArrow.clone().sub(parallel); const parallelMag = Math.abs(dot); const perpMag = perp.length(); // Green arrow at filter, along axis direction greenGroup.visible = parallelMag > 0.02; if (greenGroup.visible) { greenGroup.position.set(1.0, 0, 0); const targetDir = dot >= 0 ? dAxis.clone() : dAxis.clone().negate(); const q = new THREE.Quaternion().setFromUnitVectors(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0), targetDir.normalize()); greenGroup.quaternion.copy(q); greenGroup.scale.set(1, Math.max(0.05, parallelMag), 1); } // Grey arrow at starburst, along perpendicular direction greyGroup.visible = perpMag > 0.02; if (greyGroup.visible) { greyGroup.position.copy(starCenter); const q2 = new THREE.Quaternion().setFromUnitVectors(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0), perp.clone().normalize()); greyGroup.quaternion.copy(q2); greyGroup.scale.set(1, Math.max(0.05, perpMag), 1); } } function selectArrow(idx) { if (selectedArrowIdx === idx) { selectedArrowIdx = -1; } else { selectedArrowIdx = idx; } updateScene(); } function setViewMode(mode) { currentMode = mode; document.getElementById('btnUnpol').classList.toggle('active', mode === 'unpolarized'); document.getElementById('btnAfter').classList.toggle('active', mode === 'after'); updateScene(); } // ═══ UI WIRING ═══ document.getElementById('filterAxisAngle').addEventListener('input', updateScene); document.getElementById('btnUnpol').addEventListener('click', () => setViewMode('unpolarized')); document.getElementById('btnAfter').addEventListener('click', () => setViewMode('after')); // ═══ DEMO STEPS ═══ let _tweenRAF = null; function tweenSlider(target, duration, cb) { const slider = document.getElementById('filterAxisAngle'); const start = parseFloat(slider.value); const t0 = performance.now(); if (_tweenRAF) cancelAnimationFrame(_tweenRAF); function tick() { const t = Math.min(1, (performance.now() - t0) / duration); const ease = t * (2 - t); slider.value = Math.round(start + (target - start) * ease); updateScene(); if (t < 1) _tweenRAF = requestAnimationFrame(tick); else if (cb) cb(); } tick(); } function goToStep(n) { selectedArrowIdx = -1; switch (n) { case 0: setViewMode('unpolarized'); tweenSlider(90, 400); break; case 1: setViewMode('after'); tweenSlider(90, 400); break; case 2: setViewMode('after'); tweenSlider(45, 600); break; case 3: setViewMode('after'); tweenSlider(90, 400, () => { selectedArrowIdx = 1; updateScene(); }); break; } } document.getElementById('step0').addEventListener('click', () => goToStep(0)); document.getElementById('step1').addEventListener('click', () => goToStep(1)); document.getElementById('step2').addEventListener('click', () => goToStep(2)); document.getElementById('step3').addEventListener('click', () => goToStep(3)); // ═══ CAMERA ══ // Near-front-on to match the flat 2D layout of the source figure setCameraView({ projection: 'perspective', azimuthDeg: 8, elevationDeg: 5, rollDeg: 0, heightFraction: 0.62 }); // Initial state updateScene(); // @FIGURE_CODE_END
